children: By David Smagalla

Good morning. As the Trump administration tightens its economic squeeze on Iran, it faces a surprising weak link in its campaign to cut off the regime from the global financial system: America's own banks.

Billions of dollars of Iranian funds are flowing through clearing accounts at American banks each year, Western officials and researchers say, despite sanctions that prohibit anyone subject to U.S. law from taking part in almost all financial activity linked to Tehran.

Why it's happening: Iran accesses the accounts through foreign partners that maintain relationships with U.S. banks, part of a more than century-old system called correspondent banking that helps tie the global financial system together, while also providing Tehran with plenty of ways to secretly infiltrate it.

Moves to disrupt: The Trump administration has recently moved to put foreign banks that process dollar transactions with Iran via U.S. correspondent accounts on alert. Officials have also been pushing American banks to step up their vigilance on Iran-related transactions. But detecting them can be difficult, since Iran uses a complicated network of front companies and other means to disguise them.

Latest efforts: On Aug. 28, the U.S. Treasury identified the Emirati branch of a state-owned Egyptian bank as one of the foreign institutions it believes are helping Iran access the U.S. banking system, and said it would move to cut it off. The latest move was part of the Trump administration's new "Operation Economic Outcast," a wide-ranging pressure campaign aimed at squeezing Iran financially to force concessions and end Middle East hostilities. Washington is warning global leaders to sever ties with Iran or face secondary sanctions-the threat of being cut off from the U.S. dollar financial system entirely.

What could help: But some financial experts say Washington's efforts could have limited impact if it doesn't put more pressure on U.S. lenders to scrutinize their correspondent banking relationships more closely. The Treasury last year said it had identified about $9 billion in Iranian funds that moved through American banks in 2024, a figure that some Iran researchers say could be brought down if U.S. banks were more proactive.

Compliance
DOJ staff were told to pause antitrust work with Canadian government.

The Justice Department's antitrust division was instructed last week to pause all work with the Canadian government, according to emails reviewed by The Wall Street Journal, the latest development in the escalating trade dispute between the two countries.

In place, then withdrawn: In a Wednesday email with the subject line "Pause on Canada," Lynda Marshall, the chief of the antitrust division's international section, ordered officials to stop all cooperation on cases and engagement on policy issues with Canadian authorities. She provided no reason for the directive but said she would "circle back if the guidance changes." Marshall, in an email to staff sent later Friday afternoon, said she was mistaken and that cooperation with Canada could continue.

Turkish bank sanctioned as U.S. squeezes Iran.

The U.S. Treasury Department has sanctioned Turkey's Golden Global Bank for allegedly moving money for Iran. It is the latest action taken under the Trump administration's Operation Economic Outcast, Risk Journal's Richard Vanderford reports (free link).

Treasury on Friday said it sanctioned the bank and its subsidiaries, accusing them of moving tens of millions of dollars for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and providing Tehran with access to the global banking system.

Background: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced Operation Economic Outcast last month, calling it an "economic D-Day" while saying the U.S. approach would be measured to minimize damage to the global financial system. The new sanctions campaign is meant to strangle Iran's economy, including by putting pressure on non-Iranian entities that link it to the global economy and financial system.

A Chinese court has frozen more than 2.14 billion yuan-about $318 million-in assets linked to Netherlands-based chip maker Nexperia, Risk Journal reports (free link). The move comes amid a battle over ownership with China's Wingtech Technology, the parent company that lost control of Nexperia after Dutch authorities intervened in September last year.

Executives for Indian billionaire Gautam Adani must continue to face U.S. bribery and obstruction of justice charges, a federal judge said (free link). The court rejected a request by U.S. Justice Department prosecutors to drop the case, according to Risk Journal's Max Fillion.
The Securities and Exchange Commission proposed eliminating its pay-to-play rule, which bars investment advisers from being paid to manage money for government clients after donating.

Accident investigators probing an Amazon cargo flight crash in Miami are looking into a range of causes, including the speed of the aircraft, the weather, and whether an airport safeguard might have helped prevent the tragedy.

Oil explorers operating in the Falkland Islands face sanctions by the Argentine government after President Milei reasserted his country's claim on the Atlantic archipelago that Argentina and the U.K. went to war over more than four decades ago (free link).

Ukraine is considering legalizing its porn industry to raise tax revenues and help fund its defense needs. A bill to legalize pornography in Ukraine is awaiting its second reading in Parliament after winning a first vote in July.
The Supreme Court on Friday cleared the way for political parties to buy television advertisements at special reduced rates in the lead-up to the midterm elections.

The value threshold at which money transmitting businesses along part of the border with Mexico must report transactions. The Treasury Department's law enforcement arm has renewed an order requiring the reports.

Risk
Iran's oil dollars are drying up-and plunging it deeper into crisis.

Iran's oil export revenue is drying up as a U.S. naval blockade strangles shipments from the Persian Gulf and offshore stockpiles feeding China dwindle, putting more pressure on Tehran's battered economy.

Flow of oil recedes. No Iranian crude has crossed the blockade since it was reinstated by the U.S. Navy in mid-July, according to ship tracker Kpler. Iran is still loading small amounts of oil onto tankers, but those barrels remain trapped inside the Gulf. Meanwhile, the volume of Iranian crude already on vessels outside the blockade-a trove that is still generating revenue for Tehran-has fallen to around 29 million barrels from around 90 million barrels in mid-July and could run out next month, according to Kpler.

How Ukrainian drone strikes are pounding Russia's economy.
Ukraine's long-range drone strikes are inflicting pain on some of the most strategic sectors of the Russian economy. The costs are adding up.

Russia's reaction. By pounding refineries, shipping terminals and e-commerce warehouses, Ukraine is using economic pressure to weaken its larger foe and push Moscow to end the conflict. Russian President Vladimir Putin has declared that the strikes won't change his military aims, and Russia has hit back with its own ruthless drone strikes.

Effect felt. The Ukrainian effort is being felt by ordinary Russians-many of whom were previously shielded from the war's consequences. The broader economy was already slowing after an earlier wartime boom.

Mixed signals out of Washington are leaving private-sector firms unsure about the status of the federal government's key cybersecurity agency, which has long struggled to win over their confidence and share vital attack intelligence.

U.S. negotiators used the promise of access to Nvidia's artificial-intelligence chips to help secure a preliminary peace deal reached last year between the nations of Armenia and Azerbaijan, according to people involved in the talks.
Germany's embattled leader faces an uphill battle to save his government after a historic far-right victory on Sunday that could reshape the country's political system.
The U.S.'s status as a financial safe haven has begun to clash with President Trump's growing barrage of economic and military threats to advance his agenda.

The $1 trillion race to build data centers is driving the economy-and creating a huge new opportunity for insurers. The industry is eyeing a once-in-a-generation chance to generate tens of billions of dollars in additional income.

Belgium's revelation that it had arrested a Chinese citizen on suspicion of stealing advanced microchip technology is fueling European anxiety about Beijing's trade practices and quest for industrial secrets.
China is bolstering its biggest banks and insurers with a massive capital injection to strengthen the financial sector and shore up economic growth.
U.S. diesel prices jumped to a fresh record high as prolonged disruptions to Middle East energy flows and Russian refineries continue to tighten global supplies ahead of peak-demand season.
Electric trucking startup Windrose Technology is running low on funds and has lost about 100 Chinese employees after falling behind on wages.
Industrial production in Germany unexpectedly shrank in July, driven by sharply lower activity in the country's troubled auto sector.
China has spent years telling companies to put artificial intelligence to work. Now Beijing is preparing for the possibility that some of those workers will no longer be needed.
